content: Make a question with do or does at the
front. The main verb does not change:
You know him. -> Do you know him?
She works. -> Does she work?
he / she / it takes does; all others do.
Wh-words sit on top of the same frame:
Where do you live?
What does it mean?
BE needs no do; it moves by itself:
Are you happy?   How are you?
Contrast: many languages ask by word
order or tone. English adds the helper do.
A command is just the bare verb - no
subject, no ending:
Sit down.   Listen.   Wait.
One form, whether you tell one or many.
Add please and the order becomes a
request:  Wait, please.
Without please it can sound like an
order - so please does real work.
To say no, put don't in front:
Don't worry.
Contrast: your language may reshape the
verb for a command. English does not.
Negation finishes the do-machine: put
do/does + not before the main verb.
I know. -> I don't know.
She works. -> She doesn't work.
don't and doesn't are the normal spoken
forms; do not is for writing or emphasis.
BE says no on its own, no do needed:
It is here. -> It isn't here.
Use ONE negative per sentence:
I don't know anything.  (not 'nothing')
Contrast: some languages stack two
negatives. Standard English uses one.
One verb + four small words = the whole
control panel:
turn on / turn off   (state)
turn up / turn down  (amount)
The particle carries the meaning, not
the verb. The same grid rides other verbs.
A pronoun slips INSIDE the pair:
Turn the water off. -> Turn it off.
(not 'turn off it')
Contrast: your language may use a
separate word for each of these. English
reuses one verb and swaps the small word.
am / is / are + verb-ing = happening
right now:
I'm eating.   She's sleeping.
Present simple = always or usually
(an earlier lesson). Continuous = now:
I eat here.       (habit)
I'm eating now.   (this minute)
English makes you choose. The -ing form
is one small step from the plain verb.
Contrast: your language may use one
present for both. English marks 'now'
with be + -ing.
The past tells what already happened.
For most verbs, just add -ed:
work  ->  worked                   Press 1
play  ->  played                   Press 2
love  ->  loved                    Press 3
One shape fits everyone. I, you, she, we
and they all take the same -ed form:
We worked. She worked. They worked.
Time words pin it to the past:
yesterday, an hour ago, last week.
-ed is always spelled the same, but it
makes three sounds. Listen for them:
/t/   as in  worked
/d/   as in  called
/id/  as in  waited  (one extra beat)
The extra /id/ beat comes only after a
t or d sound (waited, ended). Other
verbs just take /t/ or /d/, no new beat.
Your language has close cousins of these.
So trust your ears: the spelling holds
still, the sound is what shifts.
Most verbs add -ed for the past. But the
most common verbs break that rule and
change shape instead:
go    ->  went                     Press 1
say   ->  said                     Press 2
take  ->  took                     Press 3
come  ->  came                     Press 4
There is no trick to guess them. You
learn each one as you meet it, the same
way you learn a new word.
In a sentence they look like this:
She went home late.                Press 1
He said no to me.                  Press 2
I took her hand.                   Press 3
They came back for us.             Press 4
More arrive card by card: break->broke,
speak->spoke, buy->bought, lose->lost.
Your language shapes its past its own way.
Few, old, and everywhere - every one you
learn, you keep for good.
To ask or deny in the past, use did -
the past form of the do-helper.
QUESTION: did goes to the front.
Did you see it?                    Press 1
Did she call you?                  Press 2
NO: did + not (didn't) before the verb.
I didn't know.                     Press 3
We didn't wait.                    Press 4
Notice: the main verb goes back to its
plain form. did already carries the past,
so you do not mark it twice.
One past marker per sentence - did OR
the past verb, never both:
Did you go?      (not: did you went)
I didn't see it. (not: didn't saw)
Be needs no did. It just adds not or
moves to the front on its own:
Were you there?   It wasn't ready.
Your language asks about the past its own
way; English always calls on did.
You now have the full set: ask, say, and
deny - in the present and the past.
